s: Compass DEF 14A filed 3 Apr 2026, ownership as of 17 Mar 2026: 8,343,912 Class A and 10,122,433 Class C shares; COMP closed $11.75 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 18,466,345 shares x $11.75 = $217M; the proxy footnote lists only outright and trust-held shares for him, no options or unvested units
did: Co-founded Compass in New York in 2012 with Ori Allon, recruiting top residential agents with equity and signing bonuses and giving them a proprietary CRM and marketing stack; grew it to the largest US brokerage by sales volume and took it public on the NYSE in April 2021.
why: Residential brokerage has no product moat, so the only scarce input is the top-producing agent. Compass bought agents outright with equity and cash advances funded by SoftBank-scale venture money, a balance sheet no incumbent partnership-structured broker could match.
obst: Compass burned cash for a decade; the April 2021 IPO priced at $18 against a $23-26 range and the stock fell below $2 in 2022 as mortgage rates froze transaction volume, forcing Reffkin to strip out roughly $320M of annualised operating expense.
turn: The 2022-2023 cost purge that produced positive free cash flow, after which Compass paid in stock for at properties Christie s International Real Estate instead of paying cash for agents one at a time.

s: Oscar Health DEF 14A filed 22 Apr 2026, ownership as of 10 Apr 2026: 2,732,292 Class B shares, 97,000 Class A shares and RSUs, and 4,400,000 options struck at $9.75; OSCR closed $32.04 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,829,290 shares x $32.04 = $90.7M plus 4,400,000 options x the $22.29 spread = $98.1M, total $189M before tax; excludes the $11.6M he realised exercising options in 2025
did: Co-founded Oscar Health in New York in 2012 with Josh Kushner to sell individual health plans on the new Affordable Care Act exchanges with an app, free telemedicine and its own claims engine; ran it as CEO to the March 2021 IPO and now serves 3.4 million members as technology chief.
why: Every incumbent insurer ran on decades-old claims systems it rented from third parties, so it could not price or serve the individual market cheaply. Oscar wrote its own claims and member stack, which let it cut administrative cost per member and bid the exchanges at prices the majors could not follow.
obst: Oscar mispriced the exchange risk pool and lost more than $200M in 2016, pulling out of Dallas and New Jersey; the stock fell from a $39 IPO price to under $3 in 2022, and Schlosser handed the CEO seat to Mark Bertolini in April 2023.
turn: The 2021 American Rescue Plan subsidy expansion, which tripled the addressable exchange population just as Oscar s own claims platform reached the scale where its cost per member fell below the incumbents.

s: Olo DEFM14A filed 8 Aug 2025 for the Thoma Bravo merger at $10.25 cash per share, completed 12 Sept 2025
m: 4,913,842 owned shares x $10.25 = $50.4M, plus the $66,721,282 disclosed for his 8,670,408 vested options and $19,083,225 for 1,861,778 RSUs and PSUs; $136M gross before tax
did: Founded Olo in New York in 2005 as GoMobo, a text-message coffee ordering service, then rebuilt it as the white-label digital ordering, payments and delivery-dispatch layer behind restaurant chains including Wingstop, Shake Shack and Denny s; IPO in March 2021, sold to Thoma Bravo for $2B cash in September 2025.
why: Chains wanted the order and the customer data on their own app, not on a marketplace that owned the guest and charged 30 percent. Olo sold the plumbing that took the order on the brand s own channel and handed it to a DoorDash driver, so it grew with delivery volume without ever paying to acquire demand.
obst: The original SMS ordering product barely grew for most of a decade and Olo nearly ran out of money twice; after the IPO it lost Subway, its largest customer, in 2021, wiping out roughly a tenth of revenue and halving the share price.
turn: The 2020 lockdowns, when Olo Dispatch became the mechanism by which chains ran their own delivery, taking the company from a niche vendor to infrastructure for over 80,000 restaurant locations.

s: Sculptor Capital DEF 14A 28 Apr 2023 Summary Compensation Table: total compensation of $37.6M for 2020, $145.8M for 2021 and $48.9M for 2022; Rithm Capital acquired Sculptor at $12.70 a share in November 2023
m: Three disclosed years of SEC-reported pay total $232M pre-tax; his 4,103,294 Class A shares and Sculptor operating-group units were cashed out in the Rithm deal; net of New York taxes on the compensation portion gives roughly $250M
did: Joined Och-Ziff in 2006 at 23 and ran its structured-credit book through the 2008 crisis, buying distressed mortgage paper that produced the firm s best returns; became chief investment officer in 2017 and chief executive of the renamed Sculptor Capital in April 2021, when his pay reached $145.8M.
why: Och-Ziff paid investment staff a formulaic share of the actual profit and loss of the book they ran rather than a discretionary bonus. A trader who compounded a concentrated distressed-credit portfolio from 2008 to 2012 therefore kept an owner s fraction of the gain without owning any of the firm.
obst: Founder Dan Och sued the firm and ran a public campaign against his pay and his promotion in 2022; the 2016 FCPA settlement over the Africa bribery case cost Sculptor $412M and triggered redemptions that cut assets under management from about $47B to roughly $32B.
turn: Och naming him heir apparent in 2018 on the strength of the credit book s returns, which converted a formulaic profit share into control of the whole firm three years later.

s: Via Transportation DEF 14A filed 8 Apr 2026, ownership as of 23 Mar 2026: 3,846,183 Class B shares and 995,833 exercisable options at $7.48 to $15.71; VIA closed $26.99 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 3,846,183 x $26.99 = $103.8M plus about $14M of in-the-money option value, plus the roughly $23M of stock he sold in the September 2025 IPO; excludes 2,051,945 unvested performance units
did: Co-founded Via in New York in 2012 with Oren Shoval to run algorithmically pooled shuttle rides in Manhattan, then turned the routing engine into software licensed to public transit agencies and school districts; listed on the NYSE in September 2025 at $46 a share.
why: Consumer ride-pooling never covered driver cost, but a city already funding paratransit and yellow buses will pay a software fee for the algorithm that fills the empty seats. That customer has a budget line, signs multi-year contracts and costs nothing to acquire twice.
obst: The consumer Via and ViaVan services never reached workable unit economics and were wound down, and pandemic lockdowns removed most ridership in 2020; the replacement business had to be sold through municipal procurement, a sales cycle measured in years.
turn: Winning large public transit and school-transport contracts, starting with Berlin s BVG, which proved agencies would buy the routing software on its own without Via operating the vehicles.

s: Sprinklr DEF 14A filed 1 May 2026: 1,574,444 Class A and 51,371,915 Class B shares, 42.0% of voting power; CXM closed $7.40 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Founded Sprinklr in New York in September 2009 and built a single platform for managing every social and messaging channel a large brand touches, selling it to chief marketing officers rather than to social-media teams; took it public on the NYSE in June 2021 at $16 a share.
why: Enterprises had bought a separate point tool for each channel and could not govern any of them centrally. Sprinklr sold one audited system of record across all of them, so a single win displaced a dozen vendors inside an account and the contract expanded by channel rather than by seat.
obst: Sprinklr bought more than a dozen small tools between 2012 and 2017 and then had to rewrite them into one codebase, a multi-year rebuild that stalled growth; the stock has fallen from over $20 to under $8 since 2024 as seat expansion slowed and he handed the CEO seat to Rory Read.
turn: The 2011 to 2014 land grab of Fortune 100 logos, taken while incumbent marketing-software vendors still treated social channels as an experiment rather than a governed enterprise system.

s: Griffon DEF 14A filed 9 Jan 2026: 2,630,251 shares, 5.6% of the company; GFF closed $100.55 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,630,251 x $100.55 = $264M; the proxy states he acquired a substantial portion of the directly held shares by investing his own money, and he realised about $54M of vesting stock in fiscal 2025
did: Joined the Griffon board in 1993 after running Ladenburg Thalmann and serving as president of Wynn Resorts, then took over as chief executive in April 2008 and rebuilt the conglomerate around Clopay garage doors and consumer tools, buying ClosetMaid, CornellCookson and Hunter Fan and selling Telephonics for $330M.
why: Clopay holds the leading share of US residential garage doors, a product replaced once a decade and specified by dealers rather than shopped on price, so margin holds through the cycle. Kramer levered that cash flow to buy unloved niche manufacturers and exited anything not first or second in its category.
obst: He took the job in April 2008 as US housing starts collapsed by more than 70 percent, taking building-products revenue with them; the AMES consumer-tools business he assembled then needed a multi-year restructuring and plant closures before it earned an acceptable margin.
turn: Selling Telephonics for $330M in 2022, which turned Griffon into a two-segment cash generator and funded a Dutch auction tender and buybacks that shrank the share count while he kept his own stock.

s: StoneX Group DEF 14A filed 26 Jan 2026, ownership as of 31 Dec 2025: 3,283,005 shares, 6.27% of the company; SNEX closed $68.47 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 3,283,005 x $68.47 = $225M, including vested options and unvested restricted shares as reported in the proxy table
did: Took over the near-dead International Assets Holding Corp in 2002 and turned it into StoneX, a clearing and hedging network for mid-size commercial clients in physical commodities, currencies and securities, through roughly 30 acquisitions including FCStone in 2009 and Gain Capital in 2020.
why: Large banks abandoned mid-size commodity hedgers - grain elevators, coffee exporters, Latin American importers - because the tickets were small and the compliance heavy. StoneX bought the orphaned desks, put them on one balance sheet and one clearing membership, and earned the spread the banks had left.
obst: FCStone arrived in 2009 carrying bad debts from the 2008 grain-price spike that had wiped out customer margin accounts, and in 2018 a single client s failed crude-oil options position cost the firm about $35M in one quarter, close to a year of net income.
turn: The 2009 all-stock merger with FCStone, which multiplied the client base and made a tiny Florida broker a clearing member across the physical commodity complex.

s: ExlService Holdings DEF 14A filed 27 Apr 2026: 3,914,904 shares, 2.56% of the company, including 885,670 shares held through a 2016 family trust; EXLS closed $37.53 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Co-founded EXL in 1999 with Vikram Talwar as an Indian back-office processor for US insurers, bought the company out of Conseco s bankruptcy in a 2002 management buyout backed by Oak Hill, listed it on Nasdaq in 2006 and, as chief executive since 2008, converted it from labour arbitrage into a data-analytics business.
why: Every offshore processor was eventually repriced to the cost of a seat in Noida. Kapoor kept the claims and underwriting data flowing through EXL s own operations and sold the analytics built on top of it, which is priced on the outcome rather than the headcount and cannot be moved to a cheaper vendor.
obst: Conseco, EXL s owner and largest customer, went bankrupt in 2002 and the founders had to buy the company out of the estate with private-equity money while the client base was in doubt; a decade later automation collapsed the price per processing seat and forced a rebuild around analytics.
turn: The 2006 purchase of Inductis, the analytics consultancy that started EXL s shift off headcount pricing and now underpins more than half of revenue.

s: Jefferies Financial Group DEF 14A filed 23 Feb 2026, which states that including earned and unearned deferred shares and options at target performance he would own 6,792,309 shares, about 3.2% of shares outstanding; JEF closed $52.33 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 6,792,309 x $52.33 = $355M; a portion is unvested performance equity that vests over three to five years
did: Ran Furman Selz s merchant banking arm and founded Jefferies Capital Partners, joined Jefferies in 2001 as chairman of its executive committee and has been President since 2013, building with Rich Handler a full-service investment bank out of a junk-bond boutique while every other US independent shrank.
why: Jefferies paid about two thirds of senior compensation in restricted stock vesting over three to five years, so the people running the firm became its largest shareholders. That let it hire entire coverage teams out of Bear Stearns, Lehman and UBS between 2008 and 2012, when the balance-sheet banks were shedding them.
obst: Jefferies nearly suffered a funding run in November 2011 when Egan-Jones cut its rating over European sovereign exposure days after MF Global failed and the stock fell more than 20 percent; the firm published its sovereign book position by position and halved it within a week to stop it.
turn: The 2012 sale to Leucadia, which gave Jefferies a permanent-capital parent, removed the overnight funding fragility that had almost killed it, and converted the two operators into large holders of the combined company.

s: Oppenheimer Holdings DEF 14A filed 13 Mar 2026, ownership as of 1 Mar 2026: 3,387,324 Class A shares, 31.9%, plus 97,172 Class B shares, 97.5%; OPY closed $115.99 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 3,484,496 shares x $115.99 = $404M; most is held through Phase II Financial L.P. and Phase II Financial Inc., his own vehicles
did: Bought control of the small brokerage Fahnestock and Co in 1985 and ran it for four decades, then in 2003 acquired Oppenheimer and Co s US retail brokerage and asset-management business from CIBC for about $250M and took its name, adding CIBC s US capital-markets arm in 2008.
why: Full-service retail brokerage was a business the wirehouses kept trying to exit and the banks kept trying to industrialise. Lowenthal bought the castoffs cheaply, largely with seller financing, and let advisers keep an unusually high payout, so the books of business came with them and the acquired revenue stuck.
obst: The 2003 CIBC purchase was funded largely with debentures payable to the seller, leaving a small Canadian-listed broker carrying the Oppenheimer cost base; the firm then had to buy back roughly $100M of frozen auction-rate securities from clients and settle with state regulators after the 2008 freeze.
turn: The 2003 CIBC transaction, which quadrupled the firm and gave an obscure discount broker one of the most recognised names on Wall Street for a price it could pay out of future earnings.

s: G-III Apparel Group DEF 14A filed 5 May 2026: 4,786,041 shares, 11% of the company; GIII closed $33.78 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Joined his father s leather-outerwear maker in 1974, took G-III public in 1989 and turned it into the licensee that designs, sources and sells Calvin Klein, Tommy Hilfiger, DKNY and Karl Lagerfeld apparel into US department stores, passing $3B of revenue; bought Donna Karan International from LVMH in 2016 for $650M.
why: Brand owners wanted category coverage without factory, inventory or markdown risk. G-III took all three on categories the licensor would not run itself, which made it the party that actually owned the department-store buying relationships and let it bolt any new brand onto the same sourcing base overnight.
obst: Its two largest licences, Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger, are owned by PVH and were withdrawn in stages between 2023 and 2025, removing roughly a quarter of revenue and forcing Goldfarb to replace rented brands with owned ones under deadline.
turn: The 2016 purchase of Donna Karan International from LVMH, which converted a licensee with no assets of its own into an owner of brands it could license out.

s: Nano Nuclear Energy DEF 14A filed 28 Jul 2026: 8,524,000 shares, 15.79% of the company, held through I Financial Ventures Group LLC; NNE closed $18.85 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 8,524,000 x $18.85 = $161M, of which 300,000 shares come from vested options; he is the sole shareholder of the holding vehicle
did: Founded Nano Nuclear Energy in New York in 2022 to develop portable microreactors, took it to Nasdaq in May 2024, and bought the KRONOS and LOKI reactor programmes out of Ultra Safe Nuclear s bankruptcy plus a HALEU fuel-transport business so the company owned real assets rather than designs.
why: Index and retail demand for a listed pure-play on small modular reactors arrived years before any reactor could be licensed. Being one of a handful of Nasdaq-quoted microreactor names let him fund a decade-long regulatory programme with equity priced at a multiple no private developer could raise against.
obst: The company has no reactor revenue and no NRC licence, and short sellers attacked it in 2024 over the thinness of its technology and its promotional disclosure; answering that required buying operating assets and hiring nuclear engineers rather than issuing more announcements.
turn: The May 2024 Nasdaq listing, which landed in the middle of the datacentre power scare and repriced every listed nuclear developer, giving him a currency to buy the Ultra Safe reactor programmes with.

s: Nasdaq DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026: 1,965,986 shares beneficially owned; NDAQ closed $98.22 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,965,986 shares and share-settled awards x $98.22 = $193M; her proxy-disclosed age is 56
did: Joined Nasdaq in 1993 as an intern, built its data products business, became chief financial officer, left to be chief financial officer of Carlyle Group in 2011, returned as president in 2014 and became chief executive in January 2017; bought Adenza for $10.5B in 2023 to turn the exchange into a software vendor.
why: Exchange matching fees are a commodity that regulators cap and rivals undercut. Friedman shifted Nasdaq s revenue to listings, index licensing, market data and bank compliance software, all of which are contractual, recur annually and reprice upward, so cyclical trading fell to a minority of the company.
obst: She was passed over for the top job and left for Carlyle in 2011 after Nasdaq s failed hostile bid for NYSE; on returning she had to defend the listings franchise against direct listings and NYSE poaching, and absorb the Adenza deal, which knocked about 12 percent off the share price the day it was announced.
turn: The January 2017 appointment as chief executive, followed by the decision to spend the balance sheet on risk and compliance software rather than on buying another exchange.
